# Optimization Principles {.unnumbered}

A working model is rarely an efficient one. Part II established how to construct ML systems that respect physical constraints; Part III addresses how to meet real-world demands on time, memory, and energy. Efficiency is also what keeps the bitter lesson affordable, because models grow with the computation available while budgets and deployment envelopes do not. Each optimization navigates a frontier, improving one metric (accuracy, latency, energy) while managing the cost to others, and each is a form of co-design. Data selection shapes the workload the algorithm sees, while compression and acceleration trade mathematical structure for physical feasibility. The principles here are the bounds and cost accounts of efficiency, which determine *why* some models are fast and affordable while others are slow and prohibitively expensive.

::: {#pri-pareto-frontier .callout-principle title="The Pareto frontier"}

**Bound**: After objective directions are normalized, a feasible point lies on the Pareto frontier exactly when no other point is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on one. No feasible design lies beyond that frontier, so moving along it improves one objective only by worsening another.

- **Quantization**: Trades numerical precision for reduced memory footprint.
- **Pruning**: Trades model capacity for smaller representations and can improve speed when the resulting sparsity or removed structures are supported by the target hardware.
- **Distillation**: Trades training compute for inference efficiency.

**Implication**: Systems engineers navigate this frontier to find the operating point appropriate to a specific deployment environment. There is no universal optimum.

:::

Navigating the Pareto frontier requires knowing *which* resource to optimize. Before selecting a technique, engineers must diagnose whether the workload is limited by computation, memory movement, or dispatch latency. Arithmetic intensity supplies the first test. The introduction derived its threshold, the ridge point, by setting the iron law's memory term equal to its compute term, and Part II placed training kernels on either side of that threshold in a roofline plot. Here the roofline becomes an explicit rule for choosing an optimization.

::: {#pri-arithmetic-intensity .callout-principle title="Arithmetic intensity law"}

**Bound**: Attainable throughput ($\AttainableComputeRate$) is no greater than the minimum of peak compute ($\PeakRate$) and DRAM bandwidth ($\Bandwidth$) times operational intensity at the cache–DRAM boundary ($I$) [@williams2009]:
$$ \AttainableComputeRate \leq \min(\PeakRate, I \times \Bandwidth) $$

Operational intensity and DRAM bandwidth must both be measured at the cache–DRAM boundary; this ideal bound excludes launch, synchronization, and other fixed overheads.

**Implication**: Adding peak compute does not raise the ideal roofline bound for a bandwidth-bound kernel. Engineers must identify whether the bottleneck is compute, bandwidth, or another system term before selecting an optimization.

:::

Many important ML kernels fall on the memory-bound side of the ridge point, especially low-reuse operations such as embedding lookup, normalization, softmax, depthwise convolution, and small-batch inference paths. Dense matrix multiplications and convolutions can instead be compute-bound when batching and hardware utilization are high. This split is a consequence of the memory wall: processor speed has historically outpaced memory bandwidth, and the cumulative gap has widened over three decades [@wulf1995; @gholami2024]. Neural networks, with their massive weight tensors and uneven temporal locality, are especially vulnerable. The arithmetic intensity law diagnoses *where* a workload sits relative to this wall. The cost of moving data explains *why* the wall is so punishing. @Tbl-bottleneck-diagnostic maps each bottleneck type to representative optimizations that address it and to changes that leave the dominant term untouched.

| **If the workload is...** |          **Dominant Term**          | **Optimization That Works**                                                | **Optimization That is Wasted**  |
|:--------------------------|:-----------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| **Memory-Bound**          |       $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$      | Quantization, pruning, batching                                            | Faster accelerator (more FLOP/s) |
| **Compute-Bound**         | $O/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$ | Better kernels, Tensor Cores, faster accelerator                           | More memory bandwidth            |
| **Latency-Bound**         |              $\Latency$             | Kernel fusion, async dispatch, bounded microbatching under the latency SLO | More FLOP/s or bandwidth alone   |

: **The Bottleneck Diagnostic**: Before optimizing, identify which iron law term dominates. Optimizing the wrong term leaves the dominant bottleneck unchanged and usually yields little or no end-to-end improvement. {#tbl-bottleneck-diagnostic tbl-colwidths="[18,18,37,27]"}

Performance is only one cost of memory movement; energy exposes a second constraint.

::: {#pri-energy-movement .callout-principle title="The energy-movement principle"}

**Decomposition**: Total workload energy depends jointly on per-event energy and event counts. In the cited 45 nm reference, moving a 32-bit value from DRAM can cost roughly 100–1,000$\times$ more energy per event than a 32-bit floating-point operation, depending on operation type [@horowitz2014].
Here, $\DataVolume$ is bytes moved and $O$ is operations executed; $\EnergyPerByteMoved$ denotes the energy per byte moved from DRAM, so one 32-bit access costs $4\,\EnergyPerByteMoved$, and $\EnergyPerOperationCompute$ denotes the energy of one 32-bit floating-point operation in the cited 45 nm technology.
$$ \TotalEnergy \approx \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved + O \times \EnergyPerOperationCompute, \qquad 4\,\EnergyPerByteMoved \gg \EnergyPerOperationCompute \quad \text{for the cited reference} $$

**Implication**: When memory movement dominates workload energy, optimization strategies should prioritize kernel fusion (avoiding intermediate off-chip traffic) and quantization (reducing data size); when computation dominates, reducing operation counts and improving arithmetic kernels remain central.

:::

Even with perfect data locality and optimal bottleneck targeting, a final constraint limits how much speedup any optimization can deliver. The introduction stated Amdahl's law for an inference pipeline whose preprocessing and postprocessing capped the gain from a faster model, and later chapters applied it case by case, to data-ingestion workers and to communication overhead in training. Stated as a principle, it bounds every optimization in this part.

::: {#pri-amdahl .callout-principle title="Amdahl's law"}

**Bound**: The maximum speedup of a system is limited by the fraction of the workload that cannot be accelerated [@amdahl1967].
Here, $\ParallelFraction$ is the fraction of baseline execution time accelerated and $G$ is that fraction's speedup, either an accelerator's gain $G_{\text{accel}}$ or a worker count $\WorkerCountWorkers$; the fixed-work model assumes the remaining fraction is unchanged and the acceleration introduces no additional overhead.
$$ \text{Speedup} = \frac{1}{(1-\ParallelFraction) + \frac{\ParallelFraction}{G}} $$

**Implication**: If 95 percent of a model runs 100$\times$ faster on a GPU, the total system speedup is capped at ~16.8$\times$. This explains *why* data loading and preprocessing often become the ultimate bottlenecks in highly optimized systems.

:::

Part III applies these principles in the order the D·A·M taxonomy suggests (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy gives the full diagnostic framework). On the data axis, @sec-data-selection asks first whether the work is necessary. Where algorithm meets machine, @sec-model-compression asks whether the remaining work can be simplified. On the machine axis, @sec-hardware-acceleration asks how to do it faster. Each chapter ends with a favorable local number (a smaller dataset, a smaller model, or a kernel placed under its roofline), and @sec-benchmarking closes the loop by testing whether those predicted savings survive end-to-end execution without violating quality constraints.
